messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John is a 60-year-old European-American male who has served in the military and currently works at a warehouse. Over the past few months, he has increasingly isolated himself from his loved ones and struggles with intense emotional distress when recalling his traumatic experiences during service. His wife notices that John avoids certain locations and activities that remind him of his time in the military. John vividly recalls a specific incident where he was part of a mission that resulted in significant loss of life among his fellow soldiers. He had come to believe that he survived only because others did not, which has led to intense feelings of guilt. When he thinks about this event, it feels as though he is reliving the terror and fear all over again. John often cannot find words to describe what happened, leaving him feeling trapped in a silent loop of memory. John's sense that the world is inherently dangerous exacerbates his maladaptive strategies. For instance, he avoids wearing clothes similar to those he wore during his deployment because they serve as potent reminders of the traumatic event. This avoidance behavior has extended to other areas of his life; he no longer visits places where he might encounter people or environments reminiscent of his military service. The guilt and loss of identity John feels have further deepened his maladaptive strategies. He avoids thinking about the incident altogether, often turning to distractions like alcohol or work at the warehouse, which temporarily alleviate his distress but do not address the underlying issues. These avoidance behaviors, in turn, reinforce his negative appraisals. For example, every time he encounters something that reminds him of the event—such as a particular uniform or a certain location—he is reminded of his survival guilt and how the world remains a dangerous place. John's wife has noticed these changes in his behavior and emotional state but finds it difficult to understand why he seems so distant and preoccupied. Recently, John had an incident at work where he became highly agitated when a colleague inadvertently mentioned something related to military operations. This led him to realize that his current coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable and that the cycle of avoidance was only worsening his condition. John’s most pressing fear is that he will never fully recover from these traumatic memories and will continue to feel disconnected from himself and others. He hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to process his experiences without being overwhelmed by guilt and terror, allowing him to regain a sense of self and reconnect with the world around him.
